title: The Great Trek of the Voortrekkers
intro: From 1836 onwards Dutch-speaking settlers left the Cape Colony by wagon train for the interior of southern Africa, seeking to live beyond British colonial administration. Their reasons included British opposition to their ownership of slaves, the abolition of slavery in 1834, and a wish for more pasture to the east.
ending: The trek led to the founding of the South African Republic, the Orange Free State and the Natalia Republic. It also displaced the Northern Ndebele and led to conflicts with the Zulu that contributed to the decline and collapse of the Zulu Kingdom.

stops.text: A Kommissietrek of 40 men and one woman, with a retinue of coloured servants and 14 wagons, set off for Natal to judge it as a homeland for Boers discontented with British rule. Petrus Lafras Uys led it.
stops.quote: On 8 September 1834, the Kommissietrek of 40 men and one woman, as well as a retinue of coloured servants, set off from Grahamstown for Natal with 14 wagons.

stops.text: The party reached the bay after about 650 kilometres, welcomed by the few British hunters and ivory traders there. The Boers made a laager in the area of the present Greyville Racecourse, and Dick King, who spoke Zulu, was sent to King Dingane at uMgungundlovu.
stops.quote: They arrived at the sweltering hot bay of Port Natal in February 1835, exhausted after their long journey.

stops.text: The party left Port Natal in early June with a stash of ivory and returned by much the same route. Jan Bantjes drew up the report on Natal, which inspired Boers at the Cape to set the Great Trek in motion.
stops.quote: The Kommissietrek left Port Natal for Grahamstown with a stash of ivory in early June 1835, following more or less the same route back to the Cape, and arrived at Grahamstown in October 1835.

stops.text: Hans van Rensburg's party, which had left the Cape in September 1835 and parted from Louis Tregardt's, was massacred here by an impi of Manukosi. Only two children, saved by a Zulu warrior, survived of its 49.
stops.quote: In late July 1836 van Rensburg's entire party of 49, except two children who were saved by a Zulu warrior, were massacred at Inhambane by an impi (a force of warriors) of Manukosi.

stops.text: Those of Tregardt's party who had settled around Soutpansberg moved on to Delagoa Bay. Most of them, Tregardt among them, died of fever.
stops.quote: Those of Tregardt's party that had set up around Soutpansberg moved on to colonise Delagoa Bay, with most of the party, including Tregardt, perishing from fever.

stops.text: Hendrik Potgieter's party was attacked by an army of 4,600 Ndebele warriors. Thirty-five armed trekkers held their laager at the cost of two men and almost all their cattle.
stops.quote: On 20 October 1836, Potgieter's party was attacked by an army of 4,600 Ndebele warriors at the Battle of Vegkop.

legs.title: Into Natal and the war with the Zulu

stops.text: Piet Retief met King Dingane to negotiate a treaty for land in present-day KwaZulu-Natal. Dingane, suspicious because of earlier Voortrekker influxes from across the Drakensberg, had Retief and seventy of his followers killed.
stops.quote: In October 1837 Retief met with Zulu King Dingane to negotiate a treaty for land in what is now Kwa-Zulu Natal.

stops.text: After Retief's party was killed, a Zulu army of 7,000 attacked Voortrekker camps in the Drakensberg foothills. In the Weenen massacre 532 people died, among them 282 Voortrekkers, of whom 185 were children, and 250 Khoikhoi and Basuto.
stops.quote: After killing Retief's delegation, a Zulu army of 7,000 impis were sent out and immediately attacked Voortrekker encampments in the Drakensberg foothills at what later was called Blaauwkrans and Weenen, leading to the Weenen massacre in which 532 people were killed

stops.text: Andries Pretorius had arrived in November to help in the defence. The trekkers fought Zulu impis here and won. Dingane's half-brother Mpande then allied with them to overthrow the king, and the Voortrekkers proclaimed the Natalia Republic.
stops.quote: A few days later on 16 December 1838, the trekkers fought against Zulu impis at the Battle of Blood River.

notes: Not in the article, so left out: Thaba Nchu, the Drakensberg crossing (the article says only that the route via Kerkenberg had not yet been discovered), Robert's Drift and the Soutpansberg (named only in passing; a drift and a range). Ithaleni (Flight Commando defeat) left out: the article gives no date and the place is only 'southwest of uMgungundlovu'. The Natalia Republic's founding has no place named. The first leg is the exploring Kommissietrek of 1834-35, which the article gives with places; the main trek begins in 1835/1836. Stops follow the article's order, not strict dates: Inhambane (July 1836) precedes Vegkop but Delagoa Bay has no date. Delagoa Bay entry delagoa-bay exists; wp given as Maputo Bay, check it resolves. Weenen has no date; Weenen/Blaauwkrans follow the Retief killing in the article. Mosega and Weenen wp titles unchecked. Grahamstown's current name is Makhanda; wp title may need checking. The Kommissietrek's return to Grahamstown is a stop because the journey came back through it.
